The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as recorded by
[[def-countable-choice]], and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal
$G$-bundle in the sense of
[[def-smooth-principal-g-bundle]]. The tangent bundle $TP$ has the canonical
smooth structure supplied by
[[thm-the-tangent-bundle-has-a-canonical-smooth-2n-manifold-structure]]. Its
**vertical subbundle** is
$$VP:=\ker(d\pi)\subseteq TP.$$
In each principal chart $U\times G$, this is the tangent bundle in the $G$
factor, so it is a smooth vector subbundle of $TP$ in the sense of
[[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]].

A **principal connection** on $P$ is a smooth vector subbundle $H\subseteq TP$
such that $T_pP=V_pP\oplus H_p$ for every $p\in P$ and
$$d(R_g)_p(H_p)=H_{pg}\qquad(p\in P,\ g\in G),$$
where $R_g(p)=pg$ is the principal right action. Thus $H$ is a smoothly varying
horizontal complement to the vertical tangent directions, invariant under the
structure-group action. This definition is conditional on a specified $H$;
it is not an existence theorem for connections on every bundle.

Let $h:TP\to H$ and $v:TP\to VP$ be the projections given by this direct-sum
decomposition. For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $P$, define the
**vertical-valued curvature** by
$$K_H(X,Y):=-v([hX,hY]),$$
where the vector-field bracket is the commutator
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. The bracket definition gives the
commutator on functions; [[thm-vector-fields-form-a-lie-algebra]] proves that
it is again a smooth vector field. In a local frame adapted to the smooth
splitting $TP=VP\oplus H$, the projections $h$ and $v$ are smooth. Therefore
$v([hX,hY])$ is a smooth vertical vector field whenever $X,Y$ are smooth.
This formula is tensorial in $X,Y$: for a smooth function $f$,
$$v([f hX,hY])=f\,v([hX,hY])-hY(f)\,v(hX)=f\,v([hX,hY]),$$
because $v(hX)=0$, and the same calculation in the second input gives
$v([hX,f hY])=f\,v([hX,hY])$, since $v(hY)=0$. It is alternating because
the bracket is alternating. To see the induced bundle map is smooth, choose
local smooth frames $E_1,\ldots,E_n$ of $TP$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_r$ of $VP$.
Tensoriality gives, for
$X=\sum_i f_iE_i$ and $Y=\sum_j g_jE_j$,
$$K_H(X,Y)=\sum_{i,j}f_i g_j K_H(E_i,E_j).$$
Each $K_H(E_i,E_j)$ is a smooth section of $VP$, so its components in the
$F_a$ frame are smooth; the displayed formula therefore has smooth local
coefficient functions. Thus the formula defines a smooth alternating bundle
map $TP\times_P TP\to VP$, independent of the local vector-field extensions
representing the tangent vectors.

This item uses the vertical-valued convention. It does not identify $VP$ with a
Lie-algebra-valued form or assert a Maurer–Cartan formula. Its axiom base
contains $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ exactly through the canonical tangent-bundle
and vector-field suppliers above; the displayed splitting and curvature
formula themselves select no objects from a family.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $G$ is a finite-dimensional real Lie group
with identity $e$, then $\mathfrak g=T_eG$, equipped with the bracket
transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields, is a finite-dimensional
real Lie algebra. It is denoted

$$\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\mathfrak g.$$

The countable-choice assumption is used exactly through the supplied
invariant-field and smooth-vector-field results.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group
with identity $e$, and write $\mathfrak g=T_eG$. For each
$X\in\mathfrak g$, the existence-and-uniqueness theorem
[[thm-one-parameter-subgroups-are-integral-curves-of-left-invariant-fields]]
supplies a unique one-parameter subgroup
$\gamma_X:\mathbb R\to G$ with $\gamma_X'(0)=X$. The **exponential map of
$G$** is the well-defined total map

$$\exp_G:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow G,\qquad \exp_G(X):=\gamma_X(1).$$

Here $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the axiom of
[[def-countable-choice|countable choice]].
The same theorem identifies $\gamma_X$ with the integral curve through $e$
of the left-invariant field $X^L$; the left translate
$t\mapsto g\gamma_X(t)$ is therefore the corresponding integral curve through
$g$. The countable-choice assumption is used exactly through that supplied
smooth invariant-field and completeness result, and evaluation at the single
time $1$ adds no choice.

A Lie group is nonempty and boundaryless. If $\dim G=0$, then
$\mathfrak g=0$ and $\exp_G(0)=e$; the definition is unchanged in dimension
one. No metric or nondegeneracy condition occurs, and $1$ is not an endpoint
of the global parameter domain $\mathbb R$. This item defines a map and asserts
no biconditional characterization.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group
with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG$.

If $\gamma:\mathbb R\to G$ is a one-parameter subgroup and
$X=\gamma'(0)$, then

$$\gamma'(t)=d(L_{\gamma(t)})_eX=X^L_{\gamma(t)}$$

for every $t\in\mathbb R$; thus $\gamma$ is the integral curve through $e$ of
the left-invariant field $X^L$. Conversely, the global integral curve through
$e$ of $X^L$ is a one-parameter subgroup. Consequently every
$X\in\mathfrak g$ determines a unique one-parameter subgroup with initial
velocity $X$.

The countable-choice assumption is used exactly through the supplied smooth
invariant-field construction and completeness theorem.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group with identity $e$ and Lie
algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG$. For $g\in G$, **conjugation by $g$** is

$$C_g:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad C_g(h)=ghg^{-1}.$$

It is a Lie-group automorphism. Indeed, associativity gives
$C_g(hk)=C_g(h)C_g(k)$, its smoothness follows from the smooth multiplication
and inversion of [[def-lie-group]], and $C_{g^{-1}}$ is its smooth inverse.
Thus its differential at the identity is the invertible linear map

$$\operatorname{Ad}_g:=d(C_g)_e:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak g.$$

Here $C_g(e)=e$, so the source and target tangent spaces are both
$\mathfrak g$; invertibility follows from
[[cor-the-differential-of-a-diffeomorphism-is-an-isomorphism]]. Write
$\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ for the group of invertible real-linear maps
of $\mathfrak g$ in the sense of
[[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]. The **adjoint map** is

$$\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g),\qquad g\longmapsto\operatorname{Ad}_g.$$

The target carries its standard smooth structure. Explicitly, if
$n=\dim\mathfrak g\geq1$, one fixed basis identifies
$\mathcal L(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g)$ with $M_n(\mathbb R)\simeq\mathbb R^{n^2}$
by [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. Under this
identification $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ is the open set
$\det\ne0$: determinant is a polynomial by
[[cor-determinant-is-a-polynomial-in-the-matrix-entries]], and invertibility
is equivalent to nonzero determinant by
[[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]. It therefore
has the restricted smooth structure from
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].
A second basis changes a matrix by $A\mapsto P^{-1}AP$, a linear
diffeomorphism, so this smooth structure is independent of the fixed basis.
If $n=0$, then $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ is the singleton containing
the unique endomorphism of the zero vector space, with its unique
zero-dimensional smooth structure; no determinant criterion is needed.

The next proposition proves that this map is a smooth group representation;
after that result it is called the **adjoint representation of $G$**.

A Lie group is nonempty and boundaryless. If $\dim G=0$, every
$\operatorname{Ad}_g$ is the unique automorphism of the zero vector space,
even when the discrete group itself is nonabelian; dimension one requires no
change. No metric, nondegeneracy, interval, endpoint, choice principle, or
biconditional is involved. Fixing one finite basis of the supplied
finite-dimensional space is a single finite existential instantiation, not a
choice from a family.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group with Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$. Its adjoint map is a group homomorphism

$$\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g),$$

and it is smooth for the standard smooth structure on
$\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$. In particular,

$$\operatorname{Ad}_{gh}=\operatorname{Ad}_g\circ\operatorname{Ad}_h,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_e=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}.$$

Thus $\operatorname{Ad}$ is a smooth finite-dimensional real representation
of $G$ on $\mathfrak g$. No choice principle is required.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.
If $F:M\to N$ and $G:N\to P$ are smooth, then $d(G\circ F)_p=dG_{F(p)}\circ dF_p$ for every $p\in M$.

derivations.claim: Write $p=s(x)a$ in an equivariant principal chart, with $s$ its local section and $a\in G$. Then $\phi_p(h)=p h=s(x)(a h)$; freeness and transitivity give bijectivity on the fibre, and this coordinate formula gives a smooth inverse. Hence $\phi_p:G\to P_x$, $h\mapsto p h$, is a diffeomorphism, so its differential at $e$ is a linear isomorphism $T_eG\to T_pP_x=V_pP$. For each $t\in\mathbb R$, the curve $c_t(s):=\gamma_Z(ts)$ is a one-parameter subgroup with initial tangent $tZ$; uniqueness in [F4] gives $c_t=\gamma_{tZ}$. Thus $\exp_G(tZ)=\gamma_{tZ}(1)=\gamma_Z(t)$. The curve $t\mapsto p\exp_G(tZ)$ is therefore $\phi_p\circ\gamma_Z$, whose derivative at zero is $d(\phi_p)_eZ$; hence $\zeta_p$ is the stated isomorphism.

In the same chart, $\zeta_p$ is the derivative of the smooth action map and its inverse is the derivative of the inverse fibre coordinate, so the family $\zeta$ and its inverse are smooth bundle maps. The complement $TP=VP\oplus H$ gives a smooth bundle projection $v$, so $\omega=\zeta^{-1}\circ v$ is a smooth fibrewise-linear 1-form. On a vertical vector $Z_P(p)=\zeta_p(Z)$, the projection is the vector itself; therefore $\omega(Z_P)=Z$. Also $v_pX=0$ exactly when $X\in H_p$, so $\ker\omega=H$.

For $g\in G$, let $R_g(p)=pg$. The maps $R_g\circ\phi_p$ and $\phi_{pg}\circ C_{g^{-1}}$ agree because $p h g=pg(g^{-1}hg)$. Differentiating at $e$ by [F6] gives $d(R_g)_p Z_P(p)=(\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}Z)_P(pg)$. Since $H$ and $VP$ are right-invariant, their projections commute with $dR_g$; applying the definition of $\omega$ yields $\omega_{pg}(dR_gX)=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega_p(X)$.

Conversely, if $\omega$ has the stated reproduction and equivariance properties, define $v:=\zeta\circ\omega$ and $H:=\ker\omega$. Reproduction gives $v\circ\zeta=\zeta$, hence $v^2=v$, $\operatorname{im}v=VP$, and $TP=VP\oplus H$. Equivariance of $\omega$ and the orbit differential identity from step 2.2 make $H$ right-invariant; smoothness of $\omega$ makes it a smooth subbundle. Thus this is a principal connection and the construction is inverse to step 2.1.

The imported curvature $K_H$ is a smooth alternating map with values in $VP$, and $\omega$ restricts to the inverse of $\zeta:P\times\mathfrak g\to VP$; consequently $\kappa_H=\omega\circ K_H$ is a well-defined smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued alternating 2-form. This is only the conversion of its target fibre; the Cartan identity is proved separately.

Let $\mathbb F$ be either $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. A
**finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $\mathbb F$** is a finite-dimensional
$\mathbb F$-vector space $\mathfrak g$ together with an $\mathbb F$-bilinear
map

$$[\ ,\ ]:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak g$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z\in\mathfrak g$,

$$[X,X]=0$$

and

$$[X,[Y,Z]]+[Y,[Z,X]]+[Z,[X,Y]]=0.$$

The first identity is **alternation** and the second is the **Jacobi
identity**. Over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, alternation is equivalent to
skew-symmetry. Indeed, bilinearity and alternation give
$0=[X+Y,X+Y]=[X,Y]+[Y,X]$, while skew-symmetry gives
$2[X,X]=0$ and hence $[X,X]=0$ because both fields have characteristic zero.
For a complex Lie algebra the bracket is required to be complex-bilinear, not
merely real-bilinear.

The definition permits the zero bracket. The zero vector space, with its
unique bracket, is a zero-dimensional Lie algebra. On a one-dimensional space,
every alternating bilinear bracket is zero: any two vectors are scalar
multiples of one vector and bilinearity reduces their bracket to $[X,X]=0$.
A vector space is nonempty because it contains zero. No basis is selected by
asserting finite-dimensionality, so the definition is choice-free. It is
purely algebraic and has no metric, nondegeneracy, manifold-boundary, or
endpoint condition.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

The graded vector space

$$ \Omega^*(M):=\bigoplus_{k\ge 0}\Omega^k(M) $$

with the wedge product is an associative graded-commutative algebra.

derivations.claim: Choose a finite basis $(e_a)_{a=1}^n$ of $\mathfrak g$ with dual basis $(e^a)_{a=1}^n$, and write $\alpha=\sum_a e_a\alpha^a$, $\beta=\sum_b e_b\beta^b$, where $\alpha^a=e^a\circ\alpha$ and $\beta^b=e^b\circ\beta$ are smooth scalar forms. Expanding the alternating permutation sum gives $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=\sum_{a,b}[e_a,e_b]\,\alpha^a\wedge\beta^b$; this finite sum is smooth and alternating, hence is in $\Omega^{p+q}(M,\mathfrak g)$.

Swapping the two blocks of $p$ and $q$ arguments in the defining permutation sum contributes the sign $(-1)^{pq}$; antisymmetry of the inner Lie bracket contributes the minus sign. Therefore $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$.

In the finite basis expansion of step 1.1, apply the scalar graded derivation rule [F3] to each $\alpha^a\wedge\beta^b$ and retain the fixed coefficient $[e_a,e_b]$. Summing the resulting finite terms gives $d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta]$.

For homogeneous $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, the same basis expansion writes $\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]$ with coefficient $[e_a,[e_b,e_c]]$ and form factor $\alpha^a\wedge\beta^b\wedge\gamma^c$. The right-hand terms have coefficients $\left[\,\left[e_a,e_b\right],e_c\right]$ and, after commuting $\beta^b$ past $\alpha^a$ using [F4], $[e_b,[e_a,e_c]]$, with the same form factor. The equality of coefficients is exactly the Lie-algebra Jacobi identity in [F1], so the graded Jacobi formula follows.

If $\mathfrak g=0$, all forms and brackets are zero; if $p=0$ or $q=0$, the same formulas use the empty wedge with sign $+1$. The finite basis in step 1.1 is one finite-dimensional coordinate calculation, not a choice from a family. The definition and identities hold on the empty manifold as well.

$$K_H(X,Y)=\sum_{i,j}f_i g_j K_H(E_i,E_j).$$

$F_a$ frame are smooth; the displayed formula therefore has smooth local

Lie-algebra-valued form or assert a Maurer–Cartan formula. Its axiom base
contains $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ exactly through the canonical tangent-bundle
and vector-field suppliers above; the displayed splitting and curvature
formula themselves select no objects from a family.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. For homogeneous $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M,\mathfrak g)$, define their **graded bracket** by

$$[\alpha\wedge\beta](X_1,\ldots,X_{p+q}) := \frac{1}{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p+q}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(p+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p+q)})].$$

Here $\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ is the space of smooth alternating $p$-linear forms with values in $\mathfrak g$, the inner bracket is the Lie-algebra bracket, and the sum is over all permutations. This is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $(p+q)$-form. It obeys graded skew-symmetry $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$, graded Jacobi

$$\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]=\left[\left[\alpha\wedge\beta\right]\wedge\gamma\right]+(-1)^{pq}\left[\beta\wedge\left[\alpha\wedge\gamma\right]\right],$$

and the exterior-derivative rule

$$d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta].$$

In particular, for $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-forms $A,B$, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$, so $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](X,Y)=[A(X),A(Y)]$. This fixes the normalization used by the Cartan curvature formula.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group with identity $e$ and Lie
algebra $\mathfrak g=T_eG$. For $g\in G$, **conjugation by $g$** is

$$C_g:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad C_g(h)=ghg^{-1}.$$

It is a Lie-group automorphism. Indeed, associativity gives
$C_g(hk)=C_g(h)C_g(k)$, its smoothness follows from the smooth multiplication
and inversion of [[def-lie-group]], and $C_{g^{-1}}$ is its smooth inverse.
Thus its differential at the identity is the invertible linear map

$$\operatorname{Ad}_g:=d(C_g)_e:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak g.$$

Here $C_g(e)=e$, so the source and target tangent spaces are both
$\mathfrak g$; invertibility follows from
[[cor-the-differential-of-a-diffeomorphism-is-an-isomorphism]]. Write
$\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ for the group of invertible real-linear maps
of $\mathfrak g$ in the sense of
[[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]. The **adjoint map** is

$$\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g),\qquad g\longmapsto\operatorname{Ad}_g.$$

$n=\dim\mathfrak g\geq1$, one fixed basis identifies

identification $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$ is the open set

after that result it is called the **adjoint representation of $G$**.

$\operatorname{Ad}_g$ is the unique automorphism of the zero vector space,
even when the discrete group itself is nonabelian; dimension one requires no
change. No metric, nondegeneracy, interval, endpoint, choice principle, or

finite-dimensional space is a single finite existential instantiation, not a
choice from a family.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group with Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$. Its adjoint map is a group homomorphism

$$\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g),$$

$\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$. In particular,

$$\operatorname{Ad}_{gh}=\operatorname{Ad}_g\circ\operatorname{Ad}_h,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_e=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}.$$

Thus $\operatorname{Ad}$ is a smooth finite-dimensional real representation
of $G$ on $\mathfrak g$. No choice principle is required.

finite-dimensional real Lie groups, with Lie algebras
$\mathfrak g=T_eG$ and $\mathfrak h=T_{e_H}H$. Then

$$dF_e:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak h$$

is a Lie-algebra homomorphism. The countable-choice assumption is used exactly
through the supplied smooth invariant-field and tangent-bracket results.

$$T_I\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)\simeq\operatorname{End}(\mathfrak g),$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its

choice axiom is used.

$\mathcal L_X\omega$ is the Lie derivative of $\omega$ regarded as an
alternating covariant tensor.

For smooth vector fields $X$ and $Y$ on $M$,

$$ \mathcal L_XY=[X,Y]. $$

operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

The shuffle convention gives $\tfrac12[\omega\wedge\omega](Z_P,Y)=[Z,\omega(Y)]$, so $\Omega_\omega(Z_P,Y)=0$. Every vertical vector is fundamental by the orbit-differential isomorphism, hence $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal.

Pullback commutes with $d$, and the fixed linear map $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$ preserves the Lie bracket by [F4]. Consequently, for fixed $g\in G$, $R_g^*\Omega_\omega=d(\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega)+\tfrac12[\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega\wedge\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega]=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\Omega_\omega$. On an overlap, differentiate $s_j(x)=s_i(x)g_{ij}(x)$ along $X\in T_xM$. countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On a principal chart, each $p\in\pi^{-1}(U_i)$ has a unique expression $p=s_i(x)h$. The associated-bundle chart therefore assigns $[s_i(x)h,v]$ the vector coordinate $\rho(h)v$. In particular $[s_i(x),\psi_i(x)]$ determines a unique smooth component $\psi_i$. If $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, then $[s_j,\psi_j]=[s_i,\rho(g_{ij})\psi_j]$; equality with $[s_i,\psi_i]$ gives $\psi_j=\rho(g_{ij}^{-1})\psi_i$.

In a finite basis of $V$, $\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ is the open subset where the determinant is nonzero, so its tangent space at the identity is $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$. Thus the differential $\rho_*$ is real-linear by [F6]. For fixed $g$, [F9] gives $\rho\circ C_{g^{-1}}=C_{\rho(g^{-1})}\circ\rho$. The derivative of target conjugation is the linear map $T\mapsto\rho(g^{-1})T\rho(g)$, while the derivative of source conjugation is $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$ by [F7]. The chain rule [F6] therefore gives $\rho_*(\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}Z)=\rho(g^{-1})\rho_*(Z)\rho(g)$. For a smooth transition $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$, differentiation of $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$ decomposes a tangent vector into the right translate of the tangent from $s_i$ and the fundamental vertical vector with generator $\theta_L(g_{ij})(X)$, by [F5]. Reproduction and equivariance in [F4] yield $A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij})$.

Put $g=g_{ij}(x)$, $Z=\theta_L(g)(X)$, and $R=\rho(g^{-1})$. Let $c$ be a smooth curve through $x$ with $c'(0)=X$, and write $h(t)=g_{ij}(c(t))$. By [F5], $h(0)=g$ and $h'(0)=d(L_g)_eZ$. For each $t\in\mathbb R$, $s\mapsto\gamma_Z(ts)$ is a one-parameter subgroup with initial tangent $tZ$, so uniqueness in [F8] and the exponential definition give $\exp_G(tZ)=\gamma_Z(t)$. Hence $k(t):=g\exp_G(tZ)=g\gamma_Z(t)$ has the same initial value and tangent as $h$. By [F6], differentiating the smooth map $q\mapsto\rho(q^{-1})$ along these curves gives the same derivative at zero. Since $k(t)^{-1}=\gamma_Z(-t)g^{-1}$, the homomorphism law [F9] and $\gamma_Z'(0)=Z$ yield $dR(X)=-\rho_*(Z)R$. Using step 1.1, step 2.1, and the adjoint-intertwining identity in step 2.1, $d\psi_j(X)+\rho_*(A_j(X))\psi_j=-\rho_*(Z)R\psi_i+R\,d\psi_i(X)+\rho_*(\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}A_i(X))R\psi_i+\rho_*(Z)R\psi_i=R\bigl(d\psi_i(X)+\rho_*(A_i(X))\psi_i\bigr)$. The two Maurer–Cartan terms cancel, and the remaining equality uses $\rho(g)R=\mathrm{id}_V$. Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. A **non-Abelian gauge datum on $M$** consists of the following specified objects.

First choose a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ that is compact in its manifold topology (every open cover has a finite subcover) and noncommutative (there are $g,h\in G$ with $gh\ne hg$). The actual group $G$, including its global form, is part of the datum. Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$ with the bracket transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields.

Choose a smooth right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$: the projection and right action are smooth, and the action is free and transitive on each fibre. There is an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of $M$ with a family of equivariant diffeomorphisms $\phi_\alpha:\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\to U_\alpha\times G$ for $\alpha\in A$, each over $U_\alpha$. Explicitly, $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\phi_\alpha=\pi$, and if $\phi_\alpha(p)=(x,g)$ then $\phi_\alpha(ph)=(x,gh)$ for every $h\in G$.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

Two smooth right principal $G$-bundles over $M$ are isomorphic over $M$ when a smooth diffeomorphism between their total spaces covers $\operatorname{id}_M$ and commutes with the right $G$-actions. To represent their isomorphism types by sets, encode a bundle by the ordered tuple of its total-space set, topology, maximal smooth atlas, projection, and right action; $M$ and $G$ are fixed parameters. Write $q\cong_M P$ when $q$ is such a bundle code isomorphic to $P$. In the cumulative hierarchy $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$, and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ at limit ordinals; $\operatorname{rank}(q)$ is the least ordinal $\alpha$ with $q\subseteq V_\alpha$. Let $r(P)$ be the least rank of a code $q\cong_M P$, and define the **bundle sector** of $P$ to be its set code
$$[P]:=\{q\in V_{r(P)+1}:q\cong_M P\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}(q)=r(P)\}.$$
The given bundle supplies a code, so minimizing the attained ranks at most its rank defines $r(P)$. Minimum-rank selection and Separation in $V_{r(P)+1}$ make $[P]$ a nonempty set. Isomorphic bundles have the same code, and equality of codes gives a common representative and hence a bundle isomorphism. This construction requires no representative choice and applies to every bundle allowed above. The datum specifies a set $\Sigma$ of admitted bundle-sector codes and requires $[P]\in\Sigma$; a model may take $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. References to the isomorphism class as a sector use this set code. The Lie algebra alone does not replace the chosen group or sector. This definition does not choose a connection, an action functional, or a quantum theory.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle for a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, with $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$. A supplied principal connection is a smooth, right-invariant complement $TP=VP\oplus H$, where $VP=\ker d\pi$; write $v:TP\to VP$ for the projection along $H$, and let $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$ be its vertical-valued curvature. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$ and $p\in P$, define the fundamental vertical vector $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$$\omega_p(X):=\zeta_p^{-1}(v_pX),\qquad X\in T_pP.$$

Then $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$ for every fixed $g\in G$. Conversely, a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form with the reproduction and equivariance properties determines the principal connection $H=\ker\omega$. The converted vertical curvature $\kappa_H:=\omega\circ K_H$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued alternating 2-form; its equality with the Cartan curvature is established in the curvature lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle with a principal connection form $\omega$ associated to $H$, using $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0p\exp_G(tZ)$ for the right action. For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Then $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal and $\operatorname{Ad}$-equivariant, and $\Omega_\omega=\omega\circ K_H$ for the imported vertical-valued curvature $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$. For any trivializing cover with smooth sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=s_i^*\Omega_\omega$. On an overlap, let $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$ be the smooth map determined by $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, and write $\theta_L(g_{ij})=g_{ij}^*\theta_L$ for the left Maurer–Cartan form. Then

$$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij}),\qquad F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i],\qquad F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i,\qquad D_{A_i}F_i=0,$$

where $D_{A_i}\eta:=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The transition equations concern changes of local sections; they do not identify an arbitrary map $M\to G$ with a global automorphism of a nontrivial bundle.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. For homogeneous $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M,\mathfrak g)$, define their **graded bracket** by

$$[\alpha\wedge\beta](X_1,\ldots,X_{p+q}) := \frac{1}{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p+q}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(p+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p+q)})].$$

Here $\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ is the space of smooth alternating $p$-linear forms with values in $\mathfrak g$, the inner bracket is the Lie-algebra bracket, and the sum is over all permutations. This is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $(p+q)$-form. It obeys graded skew-symmetry $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$, graded Jacobi

$$\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]=\left[\left[\alpha\wedge\beta\right]\wedge\gamma\right]+(-1)^{pq}\left[\beta\wedge\left[\alpha\wedge\gamma\right]\right],$$

and the exterior-derivative rule

$$d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta].$$

In particular, for $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-forms $A,B$, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$, so $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](X,Y)=[A(X),A(Y)]$. This fixes the normalization used by the Cartan curvature formula.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [[def-countable-choice]], let $G$ be a Lie
group [[def-lie-group]] with identity $e$, and write $\mathfrak g=T_eG$. A
**$\mathfrak g$-valued one-form** on $G$ means a
smooth map $\alpha:TG\to\mathfrak g$ whose restriction
$\alpha_g:T_gG\to\mathfrak g$ is linear for every $g$. Equivalently,
$V\mapsto(\pi_G(V),\alpha(V))$ is a smooth vector-bundle map
$TG\to G\times\mathfrak g$ over $\operatorname{id}_G$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-bundle-map-over-a-smooth-base-map]].

The **left Maurer--Cartan form** is the $\mathfrak g$-valued one-form
$\theta:TG\to\mathfrak g$ whose fibre map at $g$ is

$$\theta_g=d(L_{g^{-1}})_g:T_gG\longrightarrow T_eG=\mathfrak g.$$

This formula is well-defined because left translation by $g^{-1}$ sends $g$
to $e$. It is smooth and fibrewise linear because
[[prop-translations-are-diffeomorphisms-and-their-differentials-trivialize-the-tangent-bundle]]
identifies

$$TG\longrightarrow G\times\mathfrak g,\qquad V_g\longmapsto(g,\theta_gV_g)$$

as the inverse vector-bundle isomorphism to left trivialization. In
particular, $\theta_e=d(L_e)_e=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}$.

The stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly through that supplied smooth
left-trivialization theorem; the pointwise formula and passage to its second
component add no choice. A Lie group is nonempty. When $\dim G=0$, $\theta$
is the unique map between zero tangent fibres, and the definition is unchanged
in dimension one. Lie groups are boundaryless by convention, and no metric,
nondegeneracy, endpoint, or biconditional occurs.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group with Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$. Its adjoint map is a group homomorphism

$$\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g),$$

and it is smooth for the standard smooth structure on
$\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$. In particular,

$$\operatorname{Ad}_{gh}=\operatorname{Ad}_g\circ\operatorname{Ad}_h,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_e=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}.$$

Thus $\operatorname{Ad}$ is a smooth finite-dimensional real representation
of $G$ on $\mathfrak g$. No choice principle is required.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary. A **non-Abelian gauge datum on $M$** consists of the following specified objects.

First choose a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$ that is compact in its manifold topology (every open cover has a finite subcover) and noncommutative (there are $g,h\in G$ with $gh\ne hg$). The actual group $G$, including its global form, is part of the datum. Its Lie algebra is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$ with the bracket transported from left-invariant smooth vector fields.

Choose a smooth right principal $G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$: the projection and right action are smooth, and the action is free and transitive on each fibre. There is an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ of $M$ with a family of equivariant diffeomorphisms $\phi_\alpha:\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\to U_\alpha\times G$ for $\alpha\in A$, each over $U_\alpha$. Explicitly, $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\phi_\alpha=\pi$, and if $\phi_\alpha(p)=(x,g)$ then $\phi_\alpha(ph)=(x,gh)$ for every $h\in G$.

Choose a specified set $I$ of representation labels and, for each $a\in I$, a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_a$, a positive-definite Hermitian form $h_a$, and a smooth group homomorphism $\rho_a:G\to U(V_a,h_a)$. Here $U(V_a,h_a)$ is the group of complex-linear isometries of $h_a$, and a representation is the corresponding finite-dimensional group action. Its associated vector bundle is the quotient $E_a=P\times_{\rho_a}V_a$ with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho_a(g)v]$.

Two smooth right principal $G$-bundles over $M$ are isomorphic over $M$ when a smooth diffeomorphism between their total spaces covers $\operatorname{id}_M$ and commutes with the right $G$-actions. To represent their isomorphism types by sets, encode a bundle by the ordered tuple of its total-space set, topology, maximal smooth atlas, projection, and right action; $M$ and $G$ are fixed parameters. Write $q\cong_M P$ when $q$ is such a bundle code isomorphic to $P$. In the cumulative hierarchy $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$, and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ at limit ordinals; $\operatorname{rank}(q)$ is the least ordinal $\alpha$ with $q\subseteq V_\alpha$. Let $r(P)$ be the least rank of a code $q\cong_M P$, and define the **bundle sector** of $P$ to be its set code
$$[P]:=\{q\in V_{r(P)+1}:q\cong_M P\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}(q)=r(P)\}.$$
The given bundle supplies a code, so minimizing the attained ranks at most its rank defines $r(P)$. Minimum-rank selection and Separation in $V_{r(P)+1}$ make $[P]$ a nonempty set. Isomorphic bundles have the same code, and equality of codes gives a common representative and hence a bundle isomorphism. This construction requires no representative choice and applies to every bundle allowed above. The datum specifies a set $\Sigma$ of admitted bundle-sector codes and requires $[P]\in\Sigma$; a model may take $\Sigma=\{[P]\}$. References to the isomorphism class as a sector use this set code. The Lie algebra alone does not replace the chosen group or sector. This definition does not choose a connection, an action functional, or a quantum theory.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle for a finite-dimensional real Lie group $G$, with $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_eG$. A supplied principal connection is a smooth, right-invariant complement $TP=VP\oplus H$, where $VP=\ker d\pi$; write $v:TP\to VP$ for the projection along $H$, and let $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$ be its vertical-valued curvature. For $Z\in\mathfrak g$ and $p\in P$, define the fundamental vertical vector $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}p\exp_G(tZ)$. The orbit differential $\zeta_p: \mathfrak g\to V_pP$, $Z\mapsto Z_P(p)$, is a linear isomorphism, as proved below. Define the **principal connection 1-form** by

$$\omega_p(X):=\zeta_p^{-1}(v_pX),\qquad X\in T_pP.$$

Then $\omega$ is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form satisfying $\omega(Z_P)=Z$, $\ker\omega=H$, and $R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega$ for every fixed $g\in G$. Conversely, a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-form with the reproduction and equivariance properties determines the principal connection $H=\ker\omega$. The converted vertical curvature $\kappa_H:=\omega\circ K_H$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued alternating 2-form; its equality with the Cartan curvature is established in the curvature lemma.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. For homogeneous $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M,\mathfrak g)$, define their **graded bracket** by

$$[\alpha\wedge\beta](X_1,\ldots,X_{p+q}) := \frac{1}{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{p+q}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(p+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(p+q)})].$$

Here $\Omega^p(M,\mathfrak g)$ is the space of smooth alternating $p$-linear forms with values in $\mathfrak g$, the inner bracket is the Lie-algebra bracket, and the sum is over all permutations. This is a smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $(p+q)$-form. It obeys graded skew-symmetry $[\alpha\wedge\beta]=-(-1)^{pq}[\beta\wedge\alpha]$, graded Jacobi

$$\left[\alpha\wedge\left[\beta\wedge\gamma\right]\right]=\left[\left[\alpha\wedge\beta\right]\wedge\gamma\right]+(-1)^{pq}\left[\beta\wedge\left[\alpha\wedge\gamma\right]\right],$$

and the exterior-derivative rule

$$d[\alpha\wedge\beta]=[d\alpha\wedge\beta]+(-1)^p[\alpha\wedge d\beta].$$

In particular, for $\mathfrak g$-valued 1-forms $A,B$, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$, so $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](X,Y)=[A(X),A(Y)]$. This fixes the normalization used by the Cartan curvature formula.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle with a principal connection form $\omega$ associated to $H$, using $Z_P(p)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0p\exp_G(tZ)$ for the right action. For Lie-algebra-valued forms use the graded bracket defined by alternating shuffle and the Lie bracket; in degree one, $[A\wedge B](X,Y)=[A(X),B(Y)]-[A(Y),B(X)]$. Define

$$\Omega_\omega:=d\omega+\frac12[\omega\wedge\omega],\qquad D_\omega\eta:=d\eta+[\omega\wedge\eta].$$

Then $\Omega_\omega$ is horizontal and $\operatorname{Ad}$-equivariant, and $\Omega_\omega=\omega\circ K_H$ for the imported vertical-valued curvature $K_H(X,Y)=-v([hX,hY])$. For any trivializing cover with smooth sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, set $A_i=s_i^*\omega$ and $F_i=s_i^*\Omega_\omega$. On an overlap, let $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to G$ be the smooth map determined by $s_j=s_i g_{ij}$, and write $\theta_L(g_{ij})=g_{ij}^*\theta_L$ for the left Maurer–Cartan form. Then

$$A_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}A_i+\theta_L(g_{ij}),\qquad F_i=dA_i+\frac12[A_i\wedge A_i],\qquad F_j=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{ij}^{-1}}F_i,\qquad D_{A_i}F_i=0,$$

where $D_{A_i}\eta:=d\eta+[A_i\wedge\eta]$. The transition equations concern changes of local sections; they do not identify an arbitrary map $M\to G$ with a global automorphism of a nontrivial bundle.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $n\geq1$. Regarded as real Lie groups,

$$U(n)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\},\qquad SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}$$

have Lie algebras

$$\mathfrak u(n)=\{X:X^*+X=0\},\qquad \mathfrak{su}(n)=\{X\in\mathfrak u(n):\operatorname{tr}X=0\}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, $G$ a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $\pi:P\to M$ a smooth right principal $G$-bundle, and $\omega$ the principal connection 1-form of a supplied horizontal distribution. Fix a finite-dimensional complex representation $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ that is smooth, and let $E=P\times_\rho V$ be its associated vector bundle with relation $[pg,v]=[p,\rho(g)v]$. Define $\rho_*:=d\rho_e:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, where the differential is taken after viewing $\rho$ as a smooth matrix-valued map. For any open cover with smooth local sections $s_i:U_i\to P$, write $A_i=s_i^*\omega$. A smooth section $\sigma$ of $E$ has unique local components $\psi_i:U_i\to V$ given by $\sigma(x)=[s_i(x),\psi_i(x)]$. Define the **associated covariant derivative** $\nabla^\omega\sigma$ by its local components

$$
(\nabla^\omega\sigma)_i=d\psi_i+\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i,
$$

where $(\rho_*(A_i)\psi_i)(X)=\rho_*(A_i(X))\psi_i$ for $X\in TU_i$. These expressions patch to a smooth $E$-valued 1-form on $M$, independently of the chosen local sections, and satisfy $\nabla^\omega(f\sigma)=df\otimes\sigma+f\nabla^\omega\sigma$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ on $M$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [[def-countable-choice]], let $G$ be a Lie
group [[def-lie-group]] with identity $e$, and write $\mathfrak g=T_eG$. A
**$\mathfrak g$-valued one-form** on $G$ means a
smooth map $\alpha:TG\to\mathfrak g$ whose restriction
$\alpha_g:T_gG\to\mathfrak g$ is linear for every $g$. Equivalently,
$V\mapsto(\pi_G(V),\alpha(V))$ is a smooth vector-bundle map
$TG\to G\times\mathfrak g$ over $\operatorname{id}_G$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-bundle-map-over-a-smooth-base-map]].

The **left Maurer--Cartan form** is the $\mathfrak g$-valued one-form
$\theta:TG\to\mathfrak g$ whose fibre map at $g$ is

$$\theta_g=d(L_{g^{-1}})_g:T_gG\longrightarrow T_eG=\mathfrak g.$$

This formula is well-defined because left translation by $g^{-1}$ sends $g$
to $e$. It is smooth and fibrewise linear because
[[prop-translations-are-diffeomorphisms-and-their-differentials-trivialize-the-tangent-bundle]]
identifies

$$TG\longrightarrow G\times\mathfrak g,\qquad V_g\longmapsto(g,\theta_gV_g)$$

as the inverse vector-bundle isomorphism to left trivialization. In
particular, $\theta_e=d(L_e)_e=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}$.

The stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly through that supplied smooth
left-trivialization theorem; the pointwise formula and passage to its second
component add no choice. A Lie group is nonempty. When $\dim G=0$, $\theta$
is the unique map between zero tangent fibres, and the definition is unchanged
in dimension one. Lie groups are boundaryless by convention, and no metric,
nondegeneracy, endpoint, or biconditional occurs.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group with Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$. Its adjoint map is a group homomorphism

$$\operatorname{Ad}:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g),$$

and it is smooth for the standard smooth structure on
$\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$. In particular,

$$\operatorname{Ad}_{gh}=\operatorname{Ad}_g\circ\operatorname{Ad}_h,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_e=\operatorname{id}_{\mathfrak g}.$$

Thus $\operatorname{Ad}$ is a smooth finite-dimensional real representation
of $G$ on $\mathfrak g$. No choice principle is required.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

derivations.claim: Regard $M_2(\mathbb C)$ as $\mathbb R^8$. The conditions $g^*g=I$ and $\det g=1$ defining $SU(2)$ are closed equations in the matrix entries, so $SU(2)$ is closed. Each column of a unitary matrix has norm one, hence all entries have modulus at most one, so $SU(2)$ is bounded. By [F2], it is compact. The matrices $D=\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix}$ and $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ are unitary with determinant one, but $DJ=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}\ne\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}=JD$. Thus $SU(2)$ is noncommutative, and [F1] supplies its Lie-group structure. This verifies the group conditions in [A1]. The declared axiom base is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ by [A2], while [F2] uses no choice. Each Pauli matrix is Hermitian and traceless, so each $T_a$ is anti-Hermitian and traceless; [F6] puts them in $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Direct multiplication gives $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$ and $\sigma_2\sigma_1=-i\sigma_3$, hence $[T_1,T_2]=(-i/2)^2[\sigma_1,\sigma_2]=-(1/4)(2i\sigma_3)=T_3$. Since $T_3\ne0$, this also verifies that $T_1$ and $T_2$ do not commute.

The product $P=M\times SU(2)$ with right multiplication on its second coordinate is smooth, free, and transitive on each fibre, and the product chart is equivariant; [F10] therefore makes it a smooth right principal bundle. By [F8], the displayed $\omega$ is smooth. A fundamental vertical vector generated by $Z\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ at $(z,g)$ is $(0,gZ)$, and $(\theta_L)_g(gZ)=Z$, so $\omega(Z_P)=Z$. For a fixed $h\in SU(2)$, the right-translated tangent is $(X,\xi h)$; [F8] gives $(\theta_L)_{gh}(\xi h)=h^{-1}(\theta_L)_g(\xi)h=\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}((\theta_L)_g(\xi))$, and [F9] gives $\operatorname{Ad}_{(gh)^{-1}}=\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$. Therefore $\omega_{(z,gh)}(X,\xi h)=\operatorname{Ad}_{h^{-1}}\omega_{(z,g)}(X,\xi)$. Together with reproduction, [F3] shows it is a principal connection form. Its pullback along $s(z)=(z,e)$ is $A$.

The coefficients of $A$ are constant, so $dA=0$. Evaluating the bracket on $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$, [F4] gives $\tfrac12[A\wedge A](\partial_x,\partial_y)=[T_1,T_2]=T_3$ by step 1.1. Since a 2-form on $\mathbb R^2$ is determined by this value on the coordinate basis, $F=T_3dx\wedge dy$.

For the defining representation, the differential $\rho_*$ sends each tangent matrix $T\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ to the same endomorphism $T$ of $\mathbb C^2$, since $\rho$ is the matrix inclusion. Applying [F7] to a smooth $\psi:M\to\mathbb C^2$ gives the two displayed covariant derivatives. The constant matrices commute with the coordinate derivatives, and $\partial_x\partial_y\psi=\partial_y\partial_x\psi$; expansion gives $[\nabla_{\partial_x},\nabla_{\partial_y}]\psi=(T_1T_2-T_2T_1)\psi=T_3\psi$. This verifies the stated operator commutator for every smooth section in the global trivialization.
